The diplomatic center of gravity has shifted from the UN Security Council to the Gulf. This suggests a tactical retreat from multilateral legal frameworks toward pragmatic, regional security arrangements.

A coordinated push by Oman and Qatar indicates these mediators are attempting to decouple the Strait of Hormuz crisis from the broader nuclear and sanctions deadlock. While Pakistan is urging a return to the "framework peace deal" at the UNSC ([The Express Tribune](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMirgFBVV95cUxNSHh3VnJnWDNseTlZYUVyQ2lsd2RQUWVOckp3NGJvMUlHVkNpLU5naUFxRzFOczh4cGhpa3MtbDVTaU00YmZoeEpXeDJfeWVuaUVvc25EenIwRHZlTjdqbTZ2YThkeXUxVkpkUldDSE85Y3BOd2d4SlU4cktmZXVIODd2SjU0SmNfQ0hkbFVqN3pRZnFPQVpLNG8zT2dVZmdRZ0dLX241cllTMFhJMEE?oc=5)), the Gulf states are treating the maritime standoff as a separate, immediate fire to be extinguished.

The tension remains in the definition of "control." While the US maintains Iran does not control the Strait ([Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiiAFBVV95cUxQWnhyaS1tS3NVV19VeVRlS1RUeUhFblVCTkRCWmg2Z2YwTW1uR051ZFctc3F2eEcyN29hbkJkLUY3THpPVzVaYVRlcTRybGlrTGVsX3ZvTFJyQmRELVNHckg3Nk9uOUw3V2RyN2lZY0dIMW1jLWVQSUVTdXBTZGpuVE55cDBQcG01?oc=5)), the fact that Oman and Qatar are negotiating "safe passage" mechanisms effectively grants Tehran a veto over maritime traffic.
